title: $5 Billion to Point AI at American Science
hook: The White House unveiled its first 'Genesis Mission' grants — $5 billion for hundreds of AI-driven science projects, pitched in Manhattan Project terms. Critics see who's being handed the keys.
key_points: The Trump administration announced the first 'Genesis Mission' grants, per The Verge.
Roughly $5 billion is directed toward hundreds of AI-driven science projects.
The White House described the effort as 'comparable in urgency and ambition to the Manhattan Project.'
Science adviser Michael Kratsios was on Capitol Hill making the case to lawmakers.
Critics question the tech-industry framing being applied to public science funding.
Government money, not just company money, now shapes which AI research happens.
content_html: Most AI money news is about companies. This one is about the government. The Verge reports that the Trump administration unveiled the first grants under its "Genesis Mission," directing roughly $5 billion toward hundreds of AI-driven science projects, while science adviser Michael Kratsios made the case for the program to lawmakers on Capitol Hill.
extra_html:
The framing is doing a lot of work. The White House has described the effort as "comparable in urgency and ambition to the Manhattan Project" — a deliberate invocation of a wartime crash program, meant to signal both scale and national stakes. Whether the comparison holds is exactly what's being argued about; The Verge's piece is pointedly critical of the tech-industry sensibility now being applied to public science funding, and it isn't the only outlet raising that concern.

Set the rhetoric aside and there's a durable point underneath. Almost everything you read about AI's direction is decided by a handful of private labs spending their own money. Public funding works differently: it can support research with no product at the end of it, and it comes with a say in which questions get asked. Five billion dollars aimed at AI-for-science is a real change in who sets that agenda — which is precisely why the arguments about how it's spent are worth following.

related.title: Rules & Regulation
related.hook: AI raced ahead of the law, and governments are now scrambling to catch up. The big debate: how to curb real harms without strangling a genuinely useful technology.

related.title: Who Controls AI?
related.hook: The most powerful AI models are built by a handful of giant companies, because training them costs a fortune. Who holds that power — and whether 'open' AI can balance it — shapes everything.

related.title: Anthropic Launches Claude Science, an AI Lab Assistant for Researchers
related.hook: Anthropic's new Claude Science autonomously runs experiments for researchers — the same 'give it a goal, let it work' approach behind Claude Code, now aimed at biology and chemistry.

related.title: AI Helps Redesign Gene Editors to Make Fewer Mistakes
related.hook: Researchers used AlphaFold to work out which parts of a gene-editing protein cause it to cut the wrong DNA — then redesigned those parts. AI as a lab instrument, not a chatbot.
